title: CBSE assessment pattern
subject: Board Exams
summary: CBSE board papers combine theory marks with internal assessment and include competency-based questions.
points: Class 10 and 12 board papers are usually 80 marks theory with 20 marks internal assessment.
Papers mix MCQs, assertion-reason, very short, short and long answer questions, and case-based questions.
Internal assessment includes periodic tests, notebook and subject enrichment or practical work.
Passing needs both the theory and internal components, not just an overall total.
example: A case-based question gives a passage or data set and asks two or three linked questions from it.
mistakes: Assuming internal marks are guaranteed full marks.
Ignoring the internal choice given in long-answer questions.

title: ICSE and ISC: how they differ from CBSE
subject: Board Exams
summary: ICSE (Class 10) and ISC (Class 12) are CISCE exams with a wider subject spread and their own prescribed texts.
points: ICSE is the Class 10 examination and ISC the Class 12 examination, both conducted by CISCE.
Students take a larger number of subjects, grouped into compulsory and elective groups.
English and a second language are compulsory, and internal assessment varies by subject.
Prescribed literature texts and project work differ from CBSE, so NCERT chapter lists do not map exactly.
example: An ICSE student may study English literature as a separate paper with specific prescribed texts, unlike the CBSE core reader.
mistakes: Preparing ICSE literature from CBSE readers.
Assuming the CBSE marking scheme applies.

title: IB: PYP, MYP and the Diploma Programme
subject: Board Exams
summary: The International Baccalaureate runs inquiry-based programmes, with the Diploma Programme assessed on a 45-point scale.
points: PYP covers the primary years, MYP the middle years, and the DP the final two years.
DP students study six subjects, three at higher level, plus TOK, the extended essay and CAS.
Subjects are graded 1 to 7, and the core adds up to 3 points, for a maximum of 45.
Assessment includes internal assessment with criteria-based marking, not just final exams.
example: A DP student scoring 6,6,6,5,5,5 in subjects and 2 core points totals 35.
mistakes: Treating the IB syllabus as identical to NCERT — the framing and assessment differ.
Forgetting that CAS and the extended essay are requirements, not extras.

title: IGCSE and A levels (Cambridge)
subject: Board Exams
summary: IGCSE is a two-year international qualification usually taken at 16, followed by AS and A levels.
points: IGCSE is typically taken at the end of Class 10, with grades A* to G or 9 to 1.
Students choose a broad set including English, mathematics, science and humanities.
AS and A levels follow over Classes 11 and 12, with separate exam sessions.
Assessment includes coursework or practical components in several subjects.
example: A student may take IGCSE mathematics in Class 10 and then A level mathematics in Classes 11 and 12.
mistakes: Confusing IGCSE with A level — they are separate stages.
Assuming all IGCSE subjects have coursework.

title: State boards and how to use this assistant
subject: Board Exams
summary: State boards follow their own textbooks and paper patterns, which can differ from NCERT in sequence and depth.
points: Many state boards adapt NCERT, but some use their own textbooks and chapter order.
Paper pattern, marks split and internal assessment rules are set by the state board.
Concepts usually match; the sequence, examples and exam wording may not.
Tell me your board and class and I will flag when a chapter may sit differently in your syllabus.
example: A state board may teach trigonometry a year earlier than NCERT, so the class label here may not match your book.
mistakes: Assuming a state board chapter list is identical to NCERT.
Relying on an NCERT-only answer for board-specific marking.
